articles.title: China's Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending Rate Cut to 1%; Third Batch of Swap Facility Operations Approved at Over 100 Billion Yuan - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: China's Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending Rate Cut to 1%; Third Batch of Swap Facility Operations Approved at Over 100 Billion Yuan  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The People's Bank of China, together with the National Financial Regulatory Administration, the China Securities Regulatory Commission and other departments, held a symposium on the Securities, Fund and Insurance Company Swap Facility and a symposium on the Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending on November 2, to study and deploy the full use of the two structural monetary policy tools. The meetings confirmed that the Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending policy will shift from a temporary arrangement to a long-term institutional one, with the relending rate cut from 1.25% to 1%. The same day, a relevant official of the CSRC answered reporters' questions on stabilizing the market and expectations, disclosing a package of arrangements including optimization of market-support buyback rules, active ETF position building, and countercyclical adjustment of margin trading.
This is the third rate cut for the Stock Buyback and Shareholding Increase Relending tool since it was established in October 2024. The tool's initial rate was 1.75%, cut to 1.50% in May 2025, and further to 1.25% in early 2026; this round lowers it by another 0.25 percentage points to 1%. The meetings also proposed that financial institutions adhere to market-based pricing principles, reasonably add spreads on top of the relending rate and increase loan disbursements.
Looking at the tools' operation, as of the end of October this year, the swap facility had conducted two batches of operations, with 28 securities firms and fund managers participating, totaling 105 billion yuan (approximately $15.8 billion). Across the market, 902 listed companies had disclosed 1,110 buyback and shareholding increase loan announcements; including the shareholding increase loans applied for by the two state-owned capital operating companies China Reform Holdings and China Chengtong, the upper limit of applied loan quotas totaled approximately 440 billion yuan (approximately $66.2 billion), with cumulative disbursements exceeding 280 billion yuan (approximately $42.1 billion).
The CSRC official said that upon applications from relevant institutions, the CSRC, in consultation with the PBOC, has agreed to let 31 securities firms and fund managers conduct a third batch of swap facility operations, with requested quotas exceeding 100 billion yuan (approximately $15.0 billion), and operations will begin in the coming days. Compared with the more than 20 institutions in the first two batches, the participant base has expanded markedly this round.
On the buyback side, the CSRC plans four adjustments to market-support buyback rules: adding share prices falling below the IPO price ("breaking issue") as one of the conditions under which a market-support buyback may be conducted, and stipulating that market-support buybacks are not subject to the restriction that "the company's shares must have been listed for six months"; removing the restriction on declaring orders during the opening and closing call auction periods; requiring companies listed for less than 36 months whose share prices trigger market-support buyback conditions to strictly fulfill the share-price stabilization measures in their listing commitments; requiring companies with excess raised funds to implement buybacks promptly when conditions are triggered; and requiring listed companies to specify in their annual cash dividend plans a certain proportion of funds to be included in a special buyback fund, with excess raised funds included proportionally and earmarked for buyback cancellation, and gains from selling market-support buyback shares through centralized bidding also to be included in the fund.
CSRC data show that in the first 10 months of this year, 645 listed companies on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges disclosed 700 share buyback plans totaling 237.7 billion yuan (approximately $35.8 billion), of which buyback-cancellation amounted to 115 billion yuan (approximately $17.3 billion), nearly 50%; 747 companies actually implemented buybacks worth 134.5 billion yuan (approximately $20.2 billion). The planned buyback amount, actual buyback amount, cancellation amount and its proportion all hit record highs. From 2024 through the first 10 months of 2026, the cumulative disclosed buyback plan amounts and actual implementation amounts on the two exchanges both rose 50% compared with 2021-2023.
Shenzhen-listed companies have taken the lead. BOE Technology (000725.SZ) announced on November 2 that its A-share buyback plan had been completed, with approximately 191 million shares repurchased for a total payment of about 1 billion yuan (approximately $150.5 million); all repurchased shares will be cancelled to reduce registered capital. CATL (300750.SZ) disclosed that as of October 31 it had repurchased 19.6059 million shares for a total transaction amount of 5.36 billion yuan (approximately $806.5 million); the current plan envisages using no less than 20 billion yuan (approximately $3.0 billion) and no more than 40 billion yuan (approximately $6.0 billion), with the repurchased shares likewise to be cancelled. Luxshare Precision (002475.SZ) had repurchased 17.6654 million shares for about 1 billion yuan. As of November 1, Shenzhen-listed companies had 231 buyback plans in progress, with an upper limit on buyback amounts of 118.2 billion yuan (approximately $17.8 billion).
The funding side is also gathering momentum. The first batch of 18 active ETFs began fundraising on October 23 and had raised more than 35 billion yuan (approximately $5.3 billion) in total as of November 2, with 16 products hitting the 2 billion yuan (approximately $300.9 million) per-product fundraising cap and closing, and three funds completing fundraising within one day. Nine managers including Morgan Fund, E Fund and Fullgoal Fund purchased their own products through proprietary or shareholder funds, with self-purchases totaling more than 2.7 billion yuan (approximately $406.2 million). The CSRC said it will guide the 18 active ETFs that have completed fundraising to accelerate position building, study the launch of multi-asset index funds such as constant stock-bond ratio products, and promote a floating management fee model based on performance benchmarks for newly established actively managed equity funds.
On margin trading, the CSRC will work with the stock exchanges to guide securities firms in comprehensively studying, optimizing and maintaining flexibility in risk-control metrics such as the margin deposit ratio, the conversion rate of securities eligible as margin collateral, and the maintenance guarantee ratio, moderately freeing up financing capacity on the premise that risks remain generally controllable. In January 2026, the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges raised the margin deposit ratio from 80% to 100%.
| Key Data on the Two Tools | Scale | 
|---|---|
| First two batches of swap facility operations | 28 institutions, 105 billion yuan total | 
| Third batch of swap facility applications | 31 institutions, requested quotas over 100 billion yuan | 
| Upper limit of buyback and shareholding increase loan applications | About 440 billion yuan | 
| Cumulative disbursement of buyback and shareholding increase loans | Over 280 billion yuan | 
| Buyback plan amount in first 10 months | 700 plans, 237.7 billion yuan | 
| Actual buyback amount in first 10 months | 747 companies, 134.5 billion yuan | 
Note: Data sources are public disclosures by the People's Bank of China and the China Securities Regulatory Commission.
Against the market backdrop, China's A-share market has trended downward amid volatility since October this year, with the Shanghai Composite Index briefly falling below 3,600 points, and the unwinding of crowded trading structures in the tech sector triggering negative feedback in fund flows. In the first three quarters, A-share listed companies reported combined revenue of 56.74 trillion yuan, up 5.41% year on year, and net profit attributable to parent of 5.10 trillion yuan, up 7.77% year on year, with share price trends diverging from earnings trends. Over the past two years, the National Social Security Fund, basic pension funds, annuity funds and insurance funds have net purchased more than 1.5 trillion yuan of A-shares in total, and various institutional investors have recently been adding positions against the trend overall.
Dong Ximiao, chief economist at Zhaolian, said that shifting from a temporary arrangement to a long-term institutional one helps stabilize expectations across various entities and reduce the risk premium brought by policy uncertainty, driving buybacks and shareholding increases from emergency-driven to a normalized tool. Zeng Gang, dean of the Tianfu Liyan Institute of Finance, held that the rate cut lowers banks' funding costs, but the final financing price is still determined by banks adding market-based spreads on top of the 1% rate; policy can only provide a floor and cannot replace earnings improvement and corporate governance.
For the market, the highlight of this policy package lies in the tools' shift from emergency to institutionalized: the relending rate has fallen to a historic low, the institutions and quotas of the swap facility have expanded simultaneously, market-support buybacks are moving from an "option" toward a "mandatory answer," and active ETFs and optimized margin trading risk-control metrics provide support from both the funding supply and trading mechanism ends. In the short term, billion-yuan-level swap facility operations and over 35 billion yuan of active ETF position building will bring incremental funds; over the medium and long term, a higher buyback-cancellation ratio and the implementation of long-cycle assessments will affect listed companies' shareholder return mechanisms and institutional funds' allocation behavior.

articles.full_text:
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.
“Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets, so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”.
Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

articles.title: Boris Vujčić: Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world

- SPEECH
Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world
Speech by Boris Vujčić, Vice-President of the ECB, at the Central Bank of Ireland’s Financial System Conference
Dublin, 2 November 2026
Thank you to the Central Bank of Ireland for organising this conference and inviting me to speak. It is a great pleasure to be here in Dublin. Ireland illustrates why the topics of today’s event – from geopolitics to financial resilience – are timely.
Ireland has one of the most open economies in the world and it is deeply integrated into European and global markets. It is a Single Market success story, and a reminder that openness remains one of Europe’s greatest strengths.
But openness works both ways. A shift in US trade policy or a turn in global capital flows can spill over to the Irish economy particularly quickly.
What is true for Ireland is also true on a larger scale for the EU, the world’s largest trading bloc.[1] So, the question I would like to discuss today is simple to ask but harder to answer: how do we retain the benefits of an open economy in a more uncertain world increasingly shaped by geopolitics?
My answer in a single sentence is: not by retreating from openness, but by building the resilience that allows this openness to endure.
Geopolitics is becoming economics
Let me start with the environment we are facing. Geopolitical shocks are becoming more frequent. They affect growth and inflation directly, and they can threaten financial stability.
We have seen this repeatedly in recent years. Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have triggered severe disruptions in energy markets. Tariffs have renewed uncertainty and redirected global trade flows, while restrictions on exports of critical technologies and raw materials have reinforced the value of strategic autonomy (Slide 2, left-hand side). Alongside these developments, we have seen sanctions regimes, cyber threats and a step change in security and defence spending.
The result is a different macroeconomic environment. Inflation, for example, is now driven more often by supply shocks – in the past six years supply factors have played a role in three major shocks: in 2020, 2022 and 2026. And we are faced with more volatile energy prices as well as greater uncertainty about the outlook (Slide 2, right-hand side).
These shocks can also be transmitted through financial channels. Bond and equity prices may come under pressure, while investment funds could face outflows that amplify market movements.[2] Banks exposed to affected countries, sectors or markets may experience losses that weigh on capital or raise funding costs, potentially leading them to tighten lending.[3]
So far, the financial system has absorbed each of these shocks remarkably well. But financial effects can be highly non-linear and typically emerge abruptly: past resilience is no reason for complacency.  
Common in origin, uneven in impact
We cannot prevent geopolitical shocks. And pulling back from the world would not shield us from such shocks: while a fragmenting world means fewer links, it also means that those links are more concentrated. The result is less diversification and higher risk.
Energy is the clearest, and unfortunately a recurring, example.
The EU imports 57% of its energy, and almost all of its oil and gas. Before 2022, much of that came from Russia. That is why Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused the EU’s largest energy shock since the 1970s.
Europe responded. We diversified our energy supplies by increasing liquefied natural gas (LNG) import capacity and reduced our dependence on Russia. This is an important achievement. But diversification alone could not shield us when tensions erupted in the Middle East earlier this year.
This showed us that exposure is only half the story. The other half is about resilience – in other words, how well we absorb the shocks.
For the financial sector, resilience means strong capital and liquidity buffers, diversified funding, and payment and settlement systems that can withstand operational and cyber threats.
But there is also a broader, economy-wide dimension to resilience – one that is becoming increasingly important for Europe. In a more competitive and uncertain global environment, resilience requires stronger mechanisms for sharing risks and diversifying supply chains across countries and markets.
Coming back to the example of the energy shocks, they hit every Member State differently. How hard they land depends on a country’s energy mix, its trade links and the structure of its financial system. Take 2022: electricity prices for firms rose far more, and stayed high far longer, in Italy than in Spain – and part of the difference is that Spain generates much more of its power from renewables (Slide 3).
Two encouraging points follow from this. First, our energy supply is already more resilient than in 2022. As the energy mix shifts towards low-carbon sources, wholesale electricity prices have become less sensitive to gas prices, including since the start of the war in the Middle East.[4] Second, shocks that are common in origin but uneven in impact have already shown how European risk sharing can cushion country-specific effects and strengthen resilience across the EU.
This shows that the lessons about how Europe can enhance its resilience are not the same as those for other large economies such as the United States and China, which automatically benefit from scale. Europe needs to find its strength in the depth of its integration – rising above the Member State perspective towards a truly European perspective. 
Europe’s untapped strength: a truly single market
Today, fragmentation prevents us from realising our European potential. Too often, national rules, standards and procedures diverge, forcing companies to navigate multiple legal and regulatory regimes when they operate across borders. These differences act like internal tariffs: according to ECB estimates, they are equivalent to a tariff of around 67% for goods and 95% for services.[5] While this is the upper bound of estimates, the message is clear: doing business across borders within the Single Market is expensive.
One consequence is a persistent home bias, with capital staying within national borders, alongside a growing allocation of European savings to markets outside the EU.
Consider equity markets. Since 2014, estimated tariff-equivalent frictions affecting cross-border equity holdings within the euro area have fallen by around 12 percentage points. Between the euro area and the United States, the decline has been around 25 percentage points, roughly twice as much (Slide 4, left-hand side).[6] Strikingly, we are integrating faster with the United States than with each other.[7]
As a result, European savings increasingly fund US companies. There are, of course, good reasons to diversify. But in a fragmenting world, this also means greater dependence on a single external partner and leaves our own markets underdeveloped. Venture capital tells a similar story: US funds invest around six times as much as EU-based funds (Slide 4, right-hand side).[8] Foreign venture capital funds partly fill the gap, but this makes it more likely that successful European start-ups move their headquarters or intellectual property abroad, or choose to list outside the EU.
Beyond missing out on growth, a lack of integration weakens risk sharing and therefore resilience.
Let me explain why.
When a shock hits one country harder than others, integrated systems help share the burden. This holds true for energy and electricity markets, where physical interconnections and common trading hubs foster price convergence.[9] It is also true for financial markets, where investors operate across borders and regions. Cross-border investors spread gains and losses. Banks operating across borders can help sustain lending where domestic conditions are weak.
The numbers are stark. ECB research finds that around 70% of state-level output shocks in the United States are absorbed through markets and fiscal transfers, with capital markets doing most of the work. In the euro area, the overall share is far lower, at around 30%, and capital markets absorb only 5 to 10%.[10]
Two results show what that gap means in practice. European firms cut investment in response to higher oil prices. For US firms, we see no such reduction (Slide 5, left-hand side).[11] And among European firms most exposed to the COVID-19 shock, those with mostly domestic shareholders cut investment 20% more than their peers with an international shareholder base (Slide 5, right-hand side).[12]
In a fragmented Europe, investment becomes the margin of adjustment whenever a shock hits. That is a resilience problem before it is a growth problem.
Integration: our best response and the lever we control
We cannot set the trade policy of others. But the openness across borders within our Single Market is entirely within our control. Our broader aim should be to reduce barriers to trade in goods and services and complete the Single Market.
And the numbers are on our side. Reducing internal barriers to goods and services by just 2% could, in the long run, offset the projected impact of higher US tariffs on euro area GDP, estimated at around 0.7 percentage points between 2025 and 2027 (Slide 6).[13]

articles.title: Texas voters on high gas prices under Trump: ‘Probably made me go more Democrat’
articles.summary: In state where driving is part of life, president’s pledge to lower prices at the pumps cuts little iceBehind the granite countertops of Fuel City, a gas station in Dallas where taxidermy deer flank the entrance and hot tacos are served 24/7, Alina Cardenas sees first-hand that Texans are stretched thin.Drivers are filling up less, she said, while ringing people up for cigarettes and beer, and fewer people are buying a full tank. articles.full_text:
Behind the granite countertops of Fuel City, a gas station in Dallas where taxidermy deer flank the entrance and hot tacos are served 24/7, Alina Cardenas sees first-hand that Texans are stretched thin.
Drivers are filling up less, she said, while ringing people up for cigarettes and beer, and fewer people are buying a full tank. Some stop once they’ve reached $10 or $20 worth of gasoline.
Cardenas, 19, who is studying radiology at a local college, said she’s been cutting back on gas herself by staying home more and driving only to go to work and school.
“It’s just getting really expensive,” she said. “Things got harder this year.”
In a state nearly three times the size of the UK, with hundreds of thousands of miles of road, driving is an essential part of life. Commuters can spend as much as six hours a day on the road going to and from their jobs. Over much of the past year, soaring energy costs brought on by the war in Iran has made it all the more expensive.
Higher gas prices are expected to play a major role in how Texas voters will decide a key battle in the upcoming midterms. James Talarico, a state representative, is trying to best Republican Ken Paxton, a former state attorney general, to become the state’s first Democratic senator in over 30 years.
Republicans across the country are fighting an uphill battle against widespread frustration, especially among independent voters, over the economy. Recent polling shows Talarico with a slight edge over Paxton, who has been embroiled in scandals.
On Tuesday, a week before election day, Donald Trump stood in front of an oil tanker docked in Corpus Christi, Texas to announce that the first million barrels of oil from his deal with Venezuela had arrived in the state.
“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump said at a rally for Paxton in Lubbock later that day.
At another rally in Georgia later in the week, Trump touted the “hundreds of billions of dollars” that higher gas prices are bringing to American gas companies. Two of the largest, Exxon and Chevron, are based in Texas.
“We’re making a frickin’ fortune,” he told the crowd.
But in Texas, voters seem unconvinced. In the Dallas-Fort Worth area, where bumper stickers declaring “my country, not your church” speed past billboards for gun shows, drivers who spoke to the Guardian expressed deep frustration over gas prices.
Cardenas said inflated gas prices has “probably made me go more Democrat” and that she will vote for Talarico.
Tom L, 40, who declined to give his last name, said he commutes nearly six hours each day to get to his job as a data analyst in Dallas. He spends about $400 a month on gas, double what he was spending a year ago. The diesel truck that he uses for farm work now costs him around $200 a week.
“I’ve definitely had to budget tighter to compensate,” he said.
He voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election, but said he is “not sure if that was the right decision” and is unsure which Senate candidate he will support as both have their benefits and flaws.
Because Texas is a top oil producer, its residents often enjoy cheaper gas prices than the rest of the US. But the state has not been immune to the rising cost of gas amid the war in Iran. On average, a gallon of gas now costs $3.68, compared to $2.59 a year ago, according to AAA.
Diesel, which fuels the big rigs and tanker trucks that transport Texan oil, has shot up by more than 80%, from $3.18 to $5.79.
“Texans are paying less than the national average, yes, but they are also paying a lot more than they were a year ago,” said Tom Seng, a professor of energy finances at Texas Christian University. “Texans are feeling the pain just like everyone else.”
Though gas prices are just part of a slate of costs that make up everyday expenses, they tend to be the most noticeable, especially in a state where residents heavily rely on their cars for transportation.
“People on Tuesday morning, before they go to the polls … they’re not opening up their electric utility bill. They probably aren’t grocery shopping that morning,” Seng said. “But what’s the last thing that they’re probably going to see before they get to the polling place? The price of gasoline.”
Kobe Montgomery, a security guard at Fuel City in Dallas, said he uses his car to get to his job in security and to deliver for UberEats and Domino’s on the side. He has no choice but to fill up his tank whenever he needs to.
“It beats walking,” he said.
But even though he hasn’t noticed the higher cost of gas, he doesn’t plan to vote at all in the upcoming midterms, out of fear for voting for the wrong person and regretting it.
Diamond M, who declined to give her last name, said spends at least three hours on the road to get to her job as a warehouse worker. Gas, she estimates, is taking up about 20% of her take-home pay. She only fills up her tank on Friday – pay day –and forces herself to make the tank stretch the whole week.
She plans to vote for Talarico, who she believes has the best shot of lowering costs for her.
“He has a voice,” she said. “Seems like he’ll get it done.”

articles.title: ‘The content creator election’: digital streamers and TV networks face off for midterms coverage
articles.summary: Journalists such as Jim Acosta and Scott MacFarlane are now competing against their former employers for eyeballsOn Tuesday, for the first time in more than 20 years, Jim Acosta, a former CNN stalwart, will not be working for a mainstream television network on election night.Acosta, who left CNN last year after nearly 18 years at the network, is putting on his own live broadcast at the University of Virginia that will air on YouTube and his Substack platform. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, for the first time in more than 20 years, Jim Acosta, a former CNN stalwart, will not be working for a mainstream television network on election night.
Acosta, who left CNN last year after nearly 18 years at the network, is putting on his own live broadcast at the University of Virginia that will air on YouTube and his Substack platform.
And in a sign of the times, Acosta will be joined for the broadcast, hosted by the university’s Center for Politics, by another star of linear television – Katie Couric, a former Today show co-host. (Don Lemon, another CNN alum and converted new media player, may also drop by, Acosta said.)
“If folks are looking for fresh faces and a different way of doing this kind of coverage, I think it’s going to deliver that,” Acosta said.
Acosta said he will be doing his best Steve Kornacki impression, giving analysis using an interactive, touch screen battleground map just like the NBC News data guru. “Yeah, I’m going to have to go to J Crew and get some new khakis.”
Rashida Jones, who serves as chief executive of Piers Morgan’s media company Uncensored, predicted that Tuesday’s midterms will come to be remembered as “the content creator election”, when independent journalists hosting streaming broadcasts give traditional networks a run for their money.
Jones was running one of those television networks, MSNBC (now called MS Now), during the 2024 presidential election, a role she held for four years. She is working to expand Morgan’s company by launching new shows and verticals beyond the “Piers Morgan Uncensored” streaming broadcast, which has about 4.5 million subscribers on YouTube.
The plan for election night is a several-hour-long live show hosted by Morgan from Washington DC, part of a three-day stint broadcasting from the US capital city.
“Our focus is going to be making sense of what’s happening in real time,” she said in an interview. “People aren’t coming to us because they’re looking for how this part of Michigan voted. It’s more the big picture themes and takeaways. Ultimately by the end of the night, people care about where did we land, less about the individual races.”
Jones said that traditional television networks will be facing more competition than past election cycles. “If I’m a network that’s got a guy at a board and a ticker at the bottom, and I just assume people are going to come, I don’t know that that’s baked in and that’s a given this cycle. And I think what we see [on Tuesday] will be on a smaller scale what we see for the general election … I think it’ll be the content creator election.”
Scott MacFarlane, a veteran reporter who resigned from CBS News in March seeking “some independence”, joined the progressive MeidasTouch network as its chief Washington correspondent and will be co-hosting its live election broadcast.
MacFarlane says the streaming show will lack the bells and whistles of a traditional television election broadcast, which is the point. “There will be no teleprompters and no scripts,” he said. “It’s straight to the point, direct, conversational and heavy on original reporting.” He added that “dramatic theme music and theatrical presentations would miss the moment”.
Still, many millions of Americans will be watching a traditional television network – or their streaming off-shoot – to keep tabs on the elections. On election night 2024, an estimated 42.3 million viewers watched television coverage – though viewership is obviously lower for non-presidential years.
“There are more places than ever for people to get their news and information, but there’s no place that has the depth, the scope, and the breadth that NBC News has,” said Hallie Jackson, an NBC News anchor, who is penciled in for nine hours of live coverage as part of the network’s election team, along with Savannah Guthrie, Tom Llamas and Kristen Welker behind the desk (along with Kornacki).
Jackson said the key to election night is hydration, and a regimen of healthy eating that she began last week. “You have to pace yourself. You have to stay hydrated. You have to have a secret pack of M&Ms for your blood sugar that you can come back to every hour.”
Seni Tienabeso, vice-president of ABC News Live and Specialized Units, said the network has planned for a seven-hour-long broadcast, but could go much longer if a key call – perhaps for control of the US Senate or House – is on the horizon.
Asked how much effort is put toward the traditional television broadcast compared with digital and social media offerings, ABC News executives said the network is fully integrated. “For us, it’s about reaching the audience where they are,” Tienabeso said. “We don’t leave any of those arenas as secondary.” (The network’s coverage will also be aired on its ABC News Live digital channel, on Hulu, and on the Disney+ streaming service.)
Like most major networks and news organizations, ABC News relies on election results from the Associated Press – as well as a new voter survey conducted by the polling firm SSRS – to help make projections about key elections. Those decisions are made by a desk that is “holed off” from the rest of the newsroom, Tienabeso said, and is not primarily focused on beating rival networks. “We don’t pay attention to what competitors are doing,” he said. “Our decision desk makes the decision when they feel comfortable with their analysis of the race that they’re covering.”
On Tuesday, viewers watching CNN will be able to see the network’s decision desk in action, and will also have access to a new tool called CNN Sightline that will give insights into how a contest is leaning, based on both data and demographics. “I think it’s probably more transparency than we’ve ever had,” said David Chalian, CNN’s political director and Washington bureau chief.
CNN’s decision desk makes calls when they have at least 99.5% confidence that a certain candidate will win. “Speed is not part of that at all,” he said.
“In a time when voter confidence in elections is something that we constantly look at and is called into question, it only ups the seriousness of purpose with which we take this mission in projecting races,” Chalian added.
Chris Stirewalt, who serves as political editor for the cable network NewsNation and anchors the weekly show The Hill Sunday, said he doesn’t think that Republicans will be happy with the election results. He said that early returns from Ohio will be a good indication of whether “the rout is on” for Democrats.
Stirewalt is no stranger to election night, having been part of Fox News’ decision desk for several cycles before leaving the network in 2021. He said he values the finality of the process: “The conversation goes on and on and on, and then it’s over. And you count, look at the scoreboard, and then it’s done. I love that.”
While Acosta is best-known for his television work, he said he doesn’t miss CNN and is happy to be “starting something at the beginning” by working in creator-driven media. “And that’s kind of the exciting part of it, because who knows where this thing is going to take us?”
